title: Le dîner de travail  (The Work Dinner)

segments.t: Determined to save François Berléand's role in Dom Juan, Andréa invites director Christophe Bel to dinner. Back at her apartment, Colette prepares to go home to finish her tax audit, but Andréa convinces her to stay and gives her a spare toothbrush. Later at the restaurant, Christophe invites Andréa to his birthday party and boasts about how well he can manipulate people. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Christophe, tu ne peux pas refuser.
Mon amour-propre ne me le permet pas.
J'ai plein de choses à te raconter.
Non, je dois rentrer chez moi.
J'ai encore une grosse partie de mon rapport à rédiger.
Non, reste, s'il te plaît!
Tu t'habilles comme ça pour un dîner de travail?
Ce soir, je joue sobre et classe.
C'est un cadeau pour toi.
Comme ça tu n'auras plus besoin d'apporter le tien.
Je fête mon anniversaire demain soir au théâtre.
J'aimerais vraiment que tu viennes.
En tant que metteur en scène, tu es doué pour obtenir ce que tu veux.
Je ne suis pas mauvais.
Let's break down the scene line by line and explore the key expressions.
Christophe, tu ne peux pas refuser.
'Christophe, you cannot say no.' Andréa corners the stubborn young theatre director over the phone. The key word here means 'can', paired with 'to refuse' to make the point clear.
Mon amour-propre ne me le permet pas.
'My pride won't allow it.' She insists that she will not take no for an answer. The compound noun for self-respect or pride is joined with a hyphen.
J'ai plein de choses à te raconter.
'I have lots of things to tell you.' She promises an exciting conversation. Andréa opens with the word for 'I have' and lands on 'to tell' at the close.
Non, je dois rentrer chez moi.
'No, I have to go home.' In Andréa's apartment, Colette gets ready to leave to finish her work.
J'ai encore une grosse partie de mon rapport à rédiger.
'I still have a big part of my report to write.' She explains the crunch on her tax audit. Notice the formal verb for drafting or writing a report.
Non, reste, s'il te plaît!
'No, stay, please!' Andréa pulls her back. Andréa opens with the word for 'no' and lands on 'pleases' at the close.
Tu t'habilles comme ça pour un dîner de travail?
'You dress like that for a work dinner?' Looking at Andréa's chic outfit, Colette asks suspiciously. The reflexive verb for getting dressed takes the preposition for like this.
Ce soir, je joue sobre et classe.
'Tonight, I play it sober and classy.' Andréa explains her strategy for charming the young director.
C'est un cadeau pour toi.
'It is a present for you.' To make Colette feel at home, Andréa hands her a small package containing a spare toothbrush.
Comme ça tu n'auras plus besoin d'apporter le tien.
'That way you won't need to bring your own anymore.' Andréa smiles warmly. The conjunction for that way is followed by the future tense.
Je fête mon anniversaire demain soir au théâtre.
'I celebrate my birthday tomorrow evening at the theatre.' Later at the restaurant, Christophe brings up his plans.
J'aimerais vraiment que tu viennes.
'I would really like you to come.' He looks across the table and adds warmly. The key word here means 'I would like', paired with 'come' to make the point clear.
En tant que metteur en scène, tu es doué pour obtenir ce que tu veux.
'As a director, you are gifted at getting what you want.' Andréa flatters him with a sharp observation. The adverb meaning 'so much' sharpens the verb for 'are' here.
Je ne suis pas mauvais.
'I am not bad.' Christophe smirks with false modesty. The negation wraps around the verb to be. Now let's listen to the whole dialogue once again from beginning to end.

Mon amour-propre ne me le permet pas.

En tant que metteur en scène, tu es doué pour obtenir ce que tu veux.

Andréa thinks she can charm Christophe into saving the play, while Colette is slowly moving into her apartment. Keep the phrase for pride in mind: love of oneself. Join us in the next scene to see what happens next.
